content: Trichinosis, also known as trichinellosis or trichiniasis, is a parasitic disease caused by consuming raw or undercooked pork and wild game products that are infected with the larvae of Trichinella species. The disease can be classified into asymptomatic, abortive, mild, pronounced, and severe forms, depending on the severity of symptoms and the density of larvae. The transmission of Trichinella to humans typically occurs through the ingestion of undercooked meat containing cysts of the parasite. Once ingested, exposure to gastric acid and pepsin in the stomach releases the larvae from the cysts, allowing them to invade the mucosa of the small intestine. In the intestines, the cysts rupture, and the larvae develop into adult roundworms. These organisms can migrate to and invade muscle tissues, including the heart and diaphragm, and may also affect the lungs and brain. Trichinosis must be differentiated from other conditions such as influenza, salmonella, shigella, eosinophilia-myalgia syndromes, tissue parasitosis, glomerulonephritis, serum sickness, infectious meningitis and encephalitis, leptospirosis, bacterial endocarditis, and typhus exanthematicus. Globally, approximately 10,000 cases of trichinosis are reported annually. The disease is rare in developed countries but remains more common in developing regions. Risk factors for trichinosis include consuming raw or undercooked meat, informal meat transportation, age, consumption of antimicrobial-free or organic pork, and hunting practices. If untreated, symptoms of trichinosis can manifest within 1–2 days of infection. Patients may develop periorbital edema, muscle pain, and fever. Complications can involve the cardiovascular, neurological, ocular, respiratory, and digestive systems. However, most individuals with trichinosis are asymptomatic, and the infection is often self-limiting. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is generally favorable. The diagnosis of trichinosis is based on criteria established by the European Center for Disease Control, which includes a combination of clinical, laboratory, and epidemiological findings. A history of gastrointestinal symptoms, muscle pain, fever, and recent consumption of undercooked meat (such as pork, wild boar, or bear) is suggestive of trichinosis. Common physical examination findings include periorbital edema and splinter hemorrhages. Laboratory findings may reveal eosinophilia, elevated muscle enzymes, and anti-Trichinella IgG antibodies. Muscle biopsy can confirm the diagnosis. The primary treatment for trichinosis involves the use of anthelmintic drugs such as albendazole or mebendazole. Prevention is best achieved by cooking meat to safe internal temperatures. Using a food thermometer ensures that the internal temperature of the meat is high enough to kill the parasites. Historically, Trichinella spiralis was first identified in 1835 by James Paget, an English medical student. In 1846, Joseph Leidy, an American paleontologist, established the link between undercooked meat and trichinosis. Numerous outbreaks have been associated with the consumption of infected pork, wild boar, and bear meat. The pathophysiology of trichinosis involves the ingestion of undercooked meat containing Trichinella cysts. Gastric acid and pepsin release the larvae, which invade the small bowel mucosa and develop into adult worms. The adult worms have a lifespan of approximately four weeks in the small intestine. After one week, female worms release larvae that migrate through the bloodstream to voluntary muscles, where they encyst. Microscopic histopathological analysis of muscle tissue reveals characteristic findings, including a collagen capsule containing larvae surrounded by cellular infiltrates. The most common cause of trichinosis is Trichinella spiralis. Less common causes include T. britovi, T. nativa, T. pseudospiralis, T. papuae, T. nelsoni, T. murrelli, and T. zimbabwensis.
